topic: Measure: descriptive statistics, probability and distributions

notes.front: How does the handbook define the mean of a data set?
notes.back: The sum of the data points divided by the number of data points: Ȳ = ΣYᵢ/N.
notes.explanation: It is the value most commonly referred to as the average, and the handbook uses "average" as a synonym for it.
notes.example: Like five cycle times of 4, 5, 5, 6 and 10 minutes: their mean is 30 ÷ 5 = 6 minutes.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 1.3.5.1 “Measures of Location”
notes.evidence: the mean is the sum of the data points divided by the number of data points. That is, --> \[ \bar{Y} = \sum_{i=1}^{N}Y_{i}/N \] The mean is that value that is most commonly referred to as the average.

notes.front: How does the handbook define the median?
notes.back: The value of the point that has half the data smaller than it and half the data larger.
notes.explanation: It splits the sorted sample into two halves of equal size.
notes.example: Like cycle times 4, 5, 5, 6 and 10 minutes: sorted, the middle value is 5; with an even count, the handbook averages the two middle values.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 1.3.5.1 “Measures of Location”
notes.evidence: the median is the value of the point which has half the data smaller than that point and half the data larger than that point.

notes.front: How does the handbook define the mode, and is it always unique?
notes.back: The value in the sample that occurs with the greatest frequency. It is not necessarily unique.
notes.explanation: The handbook says the mode is typically used in a qualitative way, for example to see one dominant hump in the data or two or more smaller ones.
notes.example: Like defect codes logged as 3, 7, 7, 2 and 7: the mode is 7.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 1.3.5.1 “Measures of Location”
notes.evidence: the mode is the value of the random sample that occurs with the greatest frequency. It is not necessarily unique. The mode is typically used in a qualitative fashion. For example, there may be a single dominant hump in the data perhaps two or more smaller humps in the data.

notes.front: What is the range of a data set?
notes.back: The largest value minus the smallest value.
notes.explanation: It is based only on the two extreme values, so the spread near the centre of the data is not captured at all.
notes.example: Like fill weights from 496 g to 507 g: the range is 11 g, whatever the values in between.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 1.3.5.6 “Measures of Scale”
notes.evidence: the range is the largest value minus the smallest value in a data set. Note that this measure is based only on the lowest and highest extreme values in the sample. The spread near the center of the data is not captured at all.

notes.front: How does the handbook define the sample variance?
notes.back: s² = Σ(Yᵢ − Ȳ)²/(N − 1): roughly the average squared distance of the data from the mean.
notes.explanation: Squaring the distances gives greater weight to values that lie further from the mean.
notes.example: Like two readings 3 and 6 units from the mean: they add 9 and 36 to the sum, so doubling the distance quadruples the weight.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 1.3.5.6 “Measures of Scale”
notes.evidence: The variance is roughly the arithmetic average of the squared distance from the mean. Squaring the distance from the mean has the effect of giving greater weight to values that are further from the mean.

notes.front: What is the standard deviation, and why is it used alongside the variance?
notes.back: The square root of the variance; it puts the spread back into the data's own units.
notes.explanation: The variance squares the units of the data, and taking the square root restores them.
notes.example: Like fill weights in grams: the variance is in grams squared, the standard deviation in grams.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 1.3.5.6 “Measures of Scale”
notes.evidence: the standard deviation is the square root of the variance. That is, --> \( s = \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{N}(Y_{i} - \bar{Y})^{2}/(N - 1)} \) The standard deviation restores the units of the spread to the original data units (the variance squares the units).

notes.front: What is the interquartile range (IQR)?
notes.back: The upper quartile (75th percentile) minus the lower quartile (25th percentile).
notes.explanation: It is an example of a trimmed estimator: the 25% trimmed range, which drops the outer quarter of the data at each end.
notes.example: Like wait times whose lower quartile is 7 minutes and upper quartile 19 minutes: the IQR is 12 minutes.
notes.source: Wikipedia contributors, “Interquartile range” (CC BY-SA 4.0)
notes.evidence: The lower quartile corresponds with the 25th percentile and the upper quartile corresponds with the 75th percentile, so IQR = Q 3 − Q 1 . [ 1 ] The IQR is an example of a trimmed estimator , defined as the 25% trimmed range

notes.front: How is a box plot built?
notes.back: A mark at the median and a box from the lower to the upper quartile, with lines out towards the extreme points.
notes.explanation: The box covers the middle 50% of the data, which the handbook calls its "body".
notes.example: Like drawing one box per machine on a shared axis, so their medians and spreads can be compared at a glance.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 1.3.3.7 “Box Plot”
notes.evidence: Plot a symbol at the median (or draw a line) and draw a box (hence the name--box plot) between the lower and upper quartiles; this box represents the middle 50% of the data--the "body" of the data.

notes.front: What is a histogram for?
notes.back: Graphically summarising the distribution of a data set on one variable.
notes.explanation: The handbook lists what it shows: centre, spread and skewness of the data, outliers, and multiple modes.
notes.example: Like bars counting how many calls lasted 0–1, 1–2, 2–3 minutes and so on.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 1.3.3.14 “Histogram”
notes.evidence: The purpose of a histogram ( Chambers ) is to graphically summarize the distribution of a univariate data set. The histogram graphically shows the following: - center (i.e., the location) of the data; - spread (i.e., the scale) of the data; - skewness of the data; - presence of outliers; and - presence of multiple modes in the data.

notes.front: What is a run chart?
notes.back: A graph of observed data plotted in the order in which it occurred over time.
notes.explanation: Its defining feature is the time sequence of the points, rather than a summary of how often each value occurs.
notes.example: Like plotting each day's count of late deliveries in date order across a month.
notes.source: LeanOhio (Ohio Department of Administrative Services), Lean Six Sigma Terminology, ver. 2, “Run Chart”, p. 12
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does a normal probability plot show whether data are approximately normal?
notes.back: The data are plotted against a theoretical normal distribution so that normal data form an approximately straight line.
notes.explanation: The straight line is the benchmark: departures from it indicate departures from normality.
notes.example: Like lining up sorted measurements against where a normal distribution says they should fall and checking whether the points lie on a line.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 1.3.3.21 “Normal Probability Plot”
notes.evidence: The data are plotted against a theoretical normal distribution in such a way that the points should form an approximate straight line. Departures from this straight line indicate departures from normality.

notes.front: What is the sample space of an experiment?
notes.back: The set of all possible outcomes or results of that experiment or random trial.
notes.explanation: It is usually written in set notation, with the possible outcomes listed as the elements of the set.
notes.example: Like the sample space for one inspection verdict: {pass, rework, scrap}.
notes.source: Wikipedia contributors, “Sample space” (CC BY-SA 4.0)
notes.evidence: of an experiment or random trial is the set of all possible outcomes or results of that experiment. [ 4 ] A sample space is usually denoted using set notation , and the possible ordered outcomes, or sample points, [ 5 ] are listed as elements in the set.

notes.front: When are two events mutually exclusive?
notes.back: When they cannot both occur at the same time.
notes.explanation: A single coin toss is the source's example: it can land heads or tails, but not both.
notes.example: Like one inspection verdict on one part: it can be “scrap” or “first-pass good”, but not both.
notes.source: Wikipedia contributors, “Mutual exclusivity” (CC BY-SA 4.0)
notes.evidence: two events (or propositions) are mutually exclusive or disjoint if they cannot both occur at the same time. A clear example is the set of outcomes of a single coin toss, which can result in either heads or tails, but not both.

notes.front: When are two events independent?
notes.back: When their joint probability equals the product of their probabilities: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).
notes.explanation: The definition is a test on numbers: compare the probability of both happening with the product of the separate probabilities.
notes.example: Like two machines that fail for unrelated reasons: the chance both are down equals one chance times the other.
notes.source: Wikipedia contributors, “Independence (probability theory)”, “Two events” (CC BY-SA 4.0)
notes.evidence: if and only if their joint probability equals the product of their probabilities

notes.front: What does the addition rule give for the probability of A or B?
notes.back: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B).
notes.explanation: In probability, "or" allows for both events happening, which is why the overlap P(A and B) appears in the rule.
notes.example: Like a shift where P(late start) = 0.2, P(machine fault) = 0.1 and P(both) = 0.05: P(late start or fault) = 0.25.
notes.source: Wikipedia contributors, “Mutual exclusivity”, “Probability” (CC BY-SA 4.0)
notes.evidence: In probability theory, the word or allows for the possibility of both events happening. The probability of one or both events occurring is denoted P( A ∪ B ) and in general, it equals P( A ) + P( B ) – P( A ∩ B ).

notes.front: What does the multiplication rule for independent events say?
notes.back: The probability that all of the events occur is the product of their separate probabilities.
notes.explanation: For more than two events, the product condition must hold for every subset of the events, not just for all of them together.
notes.example: Like three independent checks that each pass a good part with probability 0.9: all three pass with probability 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.9.
notes.source: Wikipedia contributors, “Independence (probability theory)”, “More than two events” (CC BY-SA 4.0)
notes.evidence: This is called the multiplication rule for independent events. It is not a single condition involving only the product of all the probabilities of all single events; it must hold true for all subsets of events.

notes.front: What is the conditional probability of A given B?
notes.back: The probability of A when B is known or assumed to have occurred: P(A | B) = P(A and B) / P(B).
notes.explanation: It is the ratio of the probability of both events happening to the probability of the "given" one happening.
notes.example: Like the share of scrapped parts among those made on the night shift, rather than among all parts.
notes.source: Wikipedia contributors, “Conditional probability” (CC BY-SA 4.0)
notes.evidence: This can also be understood as the fraction of probability B that intersects with A, or the ratio of the probabilities of both events happening to the "given" one happening (how many times A occurs rather than not assuming B has occurred): P ( A ∣ B ) = P ( A ∩ B ) P ( B )

notes.front: What does the central limit theorem (CLT) state?
notes.back: Under appropriate conditions, the distribution of a normalised sample mean converges to a standard normal distribution, even if the original variables are not normal.
notes.explanation: Its reach comes from the last clause: the original variables themselves need not be normally distributed.
notes.example: Like averaging many large batches of skewed cycle times: under the right conditions, the batch averages follow a far more bell-like shape than the single times.
notes.source: Wikipedia contributors, “Central limit theorem” (CC BY-SA 4.0)
notes.evidence: under appropriate conditions, the distribution of a normalized version of the sample mean converges to a standard normal distribution . This holds even if the original variables themselves are not normally distributed .

notes.front: What is the standard error of the mean?
notes.back: The standard deviation divided by the square root of the sample size: σ/√n.
notes.explanation: It measures how widely sample means are dispersed around the population mean.
notes.example: Like a process with standard deviation 6 g sampled 9 at a time: the standard error of the mean is 6/√9 = 2 g.
notes.source: Wikipedia contributors, “Standard error” (CC BY-SA 4.0)
notes.evidence: for a given sample size, the standard error of the mean equals the standard deviation divided by the square root of the sample size. [ 1 ] In other words, the standard error of the mean is a measure of the dispersion of sample means around the population mean.

notes.front: What are the two parameters of the normal distribution, and what is the standard normal?
notes.back: Location μ and scale σ. The standard normal is the case μ = 0 and σ = 1.
notes.explanation: Every normal case can be expressed in terms of the standard one, so the handbook gives its formulas for the standard form.
notes.example: Like fill weights centred on 500 g with scale 4 g: shifting by 500 and dividing by 4 turns them into the standard normal.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 1.3.6.6.1 “Normal Distribution”
notes.evidence: where μ is the location parameter and σ is the scale parameter . The case where μ = 0 and σ = 1 is called the standard normal distribution .

notes.front: What does a z-score tell you about a raw score?
notes.back: z = (x − μ)/σ: how many standard deviations the score lies from the population mean, negative below it and positive above.
notes.explanation: Its absolute value is the distance from the mean in units of the standard deviation; its sign says which side.
notes.example: Like a shaft 0.3 mm above a mean of 20.0 mm with σ = 0.1 mm: z = +3.
notes.source: Wikipedia contributors, “Standard score”, “Calculation” (CC BY-SA 4.0)
notes.evidence: The absolute value of z represents the distance between that raw score x and the population mean in units of the standard deviation. z is negative when the raw score is below the mean, positive when above.

notes.front: What does the empirical rule (68–95–99.7) say?
notes.back: For a normal distribution, about 68%, 95% and 99.7% of values lie within one, two and three standard deviations of the mean.
notes.explanation: It is a shorthand for remembering these shares, and it applies to a normal distribution.
notes.example: Like a normal process with mean 50 and standard deviation 2: about 68% of values fall between 48 and 52.
notes.source: Wikipedia contributors, “68–95–99.7 rule” (CC BY-SA 4.0)
notes.evidence: is a shorthand used to remember the percentage of values that lie within an interval estimate in a normal distribution : approximately 68%, 95%, and 99.7% of the values lie within one, two, and three standard deviations of the mean , respectively.

notes.front: When is the binomial distribution used?
notes.back: To find the probability of x successes in N trials, each outcome labelled success or failure, with the success probability p fixed for all trials.
notes.explanation: The model assumes that p stays the same from one trial to the next.
notes.example: Like the number of defective units among 50 drawn from a line with a steady defect rate.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 1.3.6.6.18 “Binomial Distribution”
notes.evidence: These outcomes are appropriately labeled "success" and "failure". The binomial distribution is used to obtain the probability of observing x successes in N trials, with the probability of success on a single trial denoted by p . The binomial distribution assumes that p is fixed for all trials.

notes.front: What does the Poisson distribution model, and what does its parameter λ mean?
notes.back: The number of events occurring within a given time interval; λ is the average number of events in that interval.
notes.explanation: A single parameter describes the whole distribution: the average count per interval.
notes.example: Like the number of machine stoppages in an eight-hour shift.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 1.3.6.6.19 “Poisson Distribution”
notes.evidence: The Poisson distribution is used to model the number of events occurring within a given time interval. The formula for the Poisson probability mass function is --> \( p(x;\lambda) = \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{x}} {x!} \mbox{ for } x = 0, 1, 2, \cdots \) λ is the shape parameter which indicates the average number of events in the given time interval.

notes.front: What is the exponential distribution primarily used for?
notes.back: Reliability work: it models data with a constant failure rate.
notes.explanation: A constant failure rate shows up as a hazard plot that is simply equal to a constant.
notes.example: Like the time to failure of an electronic component whose chance of failing in the next hour stays the same however long it has already run.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 1.3.6.6.7 “Exponential Distribution”
notes.evidence: The exponential distribution is primarily used in reliability applications. The exponential distribution is used to model data with a constant failure rate (indicated by the hazard plot which is simply equal to a constant).

notes.front: What is the t distribution used for?
notes.back: Critical regions for many hypothesis tests, and confidence intervals.
notes.explanation: The handbook's most common example is testing whether data are consistent with an assumed process mean.
notes.example: Like checking whether ten fill weights are consistent with a target mean of 500 g.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 1.3.6.6.4 “t Distribution”
notes.evidence: The t distribution is used in many cases for the critical regions for hypothesis tests and in determining confidence intervals. The most common example is testing if data are consistent with the assumed process mean .

notes.front: How does the chi-square distribution arise?
notes.back: It results when ν independent variables with standard normal distributions are squared and summed.
notes.explanation: It is built entirely from standard normal variables: take ν of them, square each and add them up.
notes.example: Like squaring and adding four independent standard normal values: the total follows a chi-square distribution with ν = 4.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 1.3.6.6.6 “Chi-Square Distribution”
notes.evidence: The chi-square distribution results when ν independent variables with standard normal distributions are squared and summed.

notes.front: How is the F distribution built?
notes.back: As the ratio of two chi-square distributions, each first divided by its own degrees of freedom (ν₁ and ν₂).
notes.explanation: Each chi-square is scaled by its own degrees of freedom before the ratio is taken, so both ν₁ and ν₂ shape the result.
notes.example: Like dividing one scaled chi-square with 5 degrees of freedom by another with 10.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 1.3.6.6.5 “F Distribution”
notes.evidence: The F distribution is the ratio of two chi-square distributions with degrees of freedom ν 1 and ν 2 , respectively, where each chi-square has first been divided by its degrees of freedom.

notes.front: What is the Box-Cox transformation used for in the handbook's capability section?
notes.back: Transforming data from a non-normal process so that they become approximately normal.
notes.explanation: Methods based on normality pose a problem when the process distribution is not normal, and transforming the data is one remedy the handbook lists.
notes.example: Like re-expressing strongly skewed cycle times on a new scale where they look roughly bell-shaped before analysis.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.1.6 “What is Process Capability?”
notes.evidence: This poses a problem when the process distribution is not normal. Without going into the specifics, we can list some remedies. - Transform the data so that they become approximately normal. A popular transformation is the Box-Cox transformation

notes.front: For a distribution that is symmetric and unimodal, how do the mean, median and mode compare?
notes.back: They are equal: mean = median = mode.
notes.explanation: Symmetry alone makes the mean equal the median; a single peak brings the mode to the same point as well.
notes.source: Wikipedia contributors, “Skewness” (CC BY-SA 4.0)
notes.evidence: If the distribution is symmetric , then the mean is equal to the median, and the distribution has zero skewness. [ 3 ] If the distribution is both symmetric and unimodal , then the mean = median = mode .

notes.front: Does positive skew guarantee that the mean is greater than the median?
notes.back: No. Skewness is not directly related to the order of mean and median; either can be larger under positive or negative skew.
notes.explanation: So the order of the mean and median cannot, on its own, tell you the direction of skew.
notes.source: Wikipedia contributors, “Skewness” (CC BY-SA 4.0)
notes.evidence: is not directly related to the relationship between the mean and median: a distribution with negative skew can have its mean greater than or less than the median, and likewise for positive skew.

notes.front: Repair times for a machine form a symmetric distribution with a single peak. The mean is 42 minutes. What do you expect the median and mode to be?
notes.back: A) Both 42 minutes.
notes.choices:
A) Both 42 minutes
B) Both below 42 minutes
C) Both above 42 minutes
D) They cannot be judged without the raw data
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: in a symmetric distribution neither tail pulls the mean away from the median, and one peak puts the mode in the same place. D: symmetry and a single peak are enough to fix the relationship.
notes.explanation: A symmetric, unimodal distribution has mean = median = mode.
notes.source: Wikipedia contributors, “Skewness” (CC BY-SA 4.0)
notes.evidence: If the distribution is symmetric , then the mean is equal to the median, and the distribution has zero skewness. [ 3 ] If the distribution is both symmetric and unimodal , then the mean = median = mode .

notes.front: Using the interquartile range, which observations are defined as outliers?
notes.back: Those below the lower quartile minus 1.5 IQR, or above the upper quartile plus 1.5 IQR.
notes.explanation: The source's chart also separates mild outliers (beyond 1.5 IQR) from extreme ones (beyond 3 IQR).
notes.source: Wikipedia contributors, “Interquartile range”, “Outliers” (CC BY-SA 4.0)
notes.evidence: outliers are defined as mild above Q3 + 1.5 IQR and extreme above Q3 + 3 IQR. The interquartile range is often used to find outliers in data. Outliers here are defined as observations that fall below Q1 − 1.5 IQR or above Q3 + 1.5 IQR.

notes.front: A set of delivery times has a lower quartile of 20 minutes and an upper quartile of 30 minutes. Which of these observations is an outlier by the 1.5 IQR rule?
notes.back: C) 47 minutes.
notes.choices:
A) 6 minutes
B) 12 minutes
C) 47 minutes
D) 44 minutes
notes.choicesExplained: A: 6 is above the lower fence of 20 − 15 = 5. B: 12 is also inside the fences. D: 44 is below the upper fence of 30 + 15 = 45.
notes.explanation: The IQR is 30 − 20 = 10, so the fences sit 15 minutes beyond each quartile, at 5 and 45; only 47 lies outside them.
notes.source: Wikipedia contributors, “Interquartile range”, “Outliers” (CC BY-SA 4.0)
notes.evidence: Outliers here are defined as observations that fall below Q1 − 1.5 IQR or above Q3 + 1.5 IQR.

notes.front: In the handbook's box plot with fences, where are the inner fences drawn?
notes.back: At the lower quartile minus 1.5 times the IQR and the upper quartile plus 1.5 times the IQR.
notes.explanation: Outer fences at 3.0 times the IQR follow the same pattern, and points beyond them are drawn as large circles.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 1.3.3.7 “Box Plot”
notes.evidence: L1 = lower quartile - 1.5*IQ L2 = lower quartile - 3.0*IQ U1 = upper quartile + 1.5*IQ U2 = upper quartile + 3.0*IQ

notes.front: Why does the sample variance divide by n − 1 rather than n?
notes.back: Bessel's correction: using n − 1 corrects the bias in estimating the population variance from a sample.
notes.explanation: Dividing by n would give a biased estimate of the population variance; the n − 1 divisor is there to correct it.
notes.source: Wikipedia contributors, “Bessel's correction” (CC BY-SA 4.0)
notes.evidence: In estimating the population variance from a sample when the population mean is unknown, the uncorrected sample variance is the mean of the squares of deviations of sample values from the sample mean (i.e., using a multiplicative factor 1/ n ). In this case, the sample variance is a biased estimator of the population variance.

notes.front: Does the central limit theorem guarantee a good normal approximation once samples exceed about 30?
notes.back: No. That rule of thumb has no valid justification and can lead to seriously flawed inferences.
notes.explanation: The belief is listed as a misconception because it claims reliable inferences whatever the nature of the population.
notes.source: Wikipedia contributors, “Central limit theorem”, “Common misconceptions” (CC BY-SA 4.0)
notes.evidence: The misconceived belief that the theorem leads to a good approximation of a normal distribution for sample sizes greater than around 30, [ 27 ] allowing reliable inferences regardless of the nature of the population. In reality, this empirical rule of thumb has no valid justification, and can lead to seriously flawed inferences.

notes.front: An analyst draws many large samples from a clearly skewed process and plots each sample's mean. Under appropriate conditions, what does the central limit theorem lead her to expect?
notes.back: B) The distribution of the sample means will approach a normal distribution.
notes.choices:
A) The individual values in each sample will become normal
B) The distribution of the sample means will approach a normal distribution
C) The sample means will be skewed just like the process
D) Normality is guaranteed once each sample has more than 30 values
notes.choicesExplained: A: the theorem concerns means (or sums), not the raw values. C: the theorem holds even when the original variables are not normal. D: the "more than 30" rule of thumb has no valid justification.
notes.explanation: The theorem says the normalised sample mean converges in distribution to a normal, even if the original variables are not normally distributed.
notes.source: Wikipedia contributors, “Central limit theorem” (CC BY-SA 4.0)
notes.evidence: under appropriate conditions, the distribution of a normalized version of the sample mean converges to a standard normal distribution . This holds even if the original variables themselves are not normally distributed .

notes.front: How many times as many observations are needed to halve the standard error of the mean?
notes.back: Four times as many.
notes.explanation: The error shrinks with 1/√n, so cutting it tenfold would take a hundred times as many observations.
notes.source: Wikipedia contributors, “Standard error”, “Exact value” (CC BY-SA 4.0)
notes.evidence: reducing the error on the estimate by a factor of two requires acquiring four times as many observations in the sample; reducing it by a factor of ten requires a hundred times as many observations.

notes.front: Fill weights are normally distributed with a mean of 500 g and a standard deviation of 4 g. Roughly what share of fills lies between 492 g and 508 g?
notes.back: C) About 95%.
notes.choices:
A) About 50%
B) About 68%
C) About 95%
D) About 99.7%
notes.choicesExplained: A: about 50% of fills lie above the mean and 50% below; that is not the share inside a band around it. B: 68% is the share within one standard deviation (496–504 g). D: 99.7% is the share within three (488–512 g).
notes.explanation: 492 g and 508 g are two standard deviations either side of the mean, and about 95% of normal values fall within two.
notes.source: Wikipedia contributors, “68–95–99.7 rule” (CC BY-SA 4.0)
notes.evidence: approximately 68%, 95%, and 99.7% of the values lie within one, two, and three standard deviations of the mean , respectively.

notes.front: A shaft measures 12.6 mm. The population mean is 12.0 mm and the standard deviation is 0.2 mm. What is its z-score?
notes.choicesExplained: B: 0.6 mm is the raw distance, not yet divided by the standard deviation. C: the shaft is above the mean, so z is positive. A: dividing the 0.6 mm distance by the 0.2 mm standard deviation gives 3, not 0.3.
notes.explanation: z = (12.6 − 12.0)/0.2 = 3.0, positive because the shaft lies above the mean.
notes.source: Wikipedia contributors, “Standard score”, “Calculation” (CC BY-SA 4.0)
notes.evidence: The absolute value of z represents the distance between that raw score x and the population mean in units of the standard deviation. z is negative when the raw score is below the mean, positive when above.

notes.front: In a batch of panels, the probability of a scratch is 0.10, of a dent 0.05, and of both 0.02. What is the probability that a panel has a scratch or a dent?
notes.choicesExplained: C: adding 0.10 and 0.05 counts the panels with both defects twice. B: multiplying treats the question as "both", and assumes independence. D: the overlap must be subtracted, not added.
notes.explanation: P(scratch or dent) = 0.10 + 0.05 − 0.02 = 0.13; "or" includes panels with both defects, so the overlap is taken off once.
notes.source: Wikipedia contributors, “Mutual exclusivity”, “Probability” (CC BY-SA 4.0)
notes.evidence: In probability theory, the word or allows for the possibility of both events happening. The probability of one or both events occurring is denoted P( A ∪ B ) and in general, it equals P( A ) + P( B ) – P( A ∩ B ).

notes.front: Is P(A | B) generally the same as P(B | A)?
notes.back: No. The conditional probability of A given B typically differs from that of B given A.
notes.explanation: In the source's dengue example, a 90% chance of testing positive given the disease says nothing directly about the chance of the disease given a positive test.
notes.source: Wikipedia contributors, “Conditional probability” (CC BY-SA 4.0)
notes.evidence: P( A | B ) (the conditional probability of A given B ) typically differs from P( B | A ) . For example, if a person has dengue fever , the person might have a 90% chance of being tested as positive for the disease.

notes.front: What is the variance of a binomial count with n trials and success probability p?
notes.back: npq = np(1 − p), where q = 1 − p.
notes.explanation: It follows from the rule that the variance of a sum of independent random variables is the sum of their variances.
notes.source: Wikipedia contributors, “Binomial distribution”, “Expected value and variance” (CC BY-SA 4.0)
notes.evidence: The variance is: Var ⁡ ( X ) = n p q = n p ( 1 − p ) . {\displaystyle \operatorname {Var} (X)=npq=np(1-p).} This similarly follows from the fact that the variance of a sum of independent random variables is the sum of the variances.

notes.front: For a Poisson distribution, how do the mean and variance compare?
notes.back: They are equal.
notes.explanation: One number therefore fixes both the centre and the spread of the count, which the handbook uses when working out limits for counts.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.3.1 “What are Control Charts?”
notes.evidence: For a Poisson distribution the mean and variance both equal np . Hence the upper 3-sigma limit is 0.8 + 3 sqrt (0.8) = 3.48 and the lower limit is 0

notes.front: An inspector draws 50 units from a line whose defect rate is steady and counts how many are defective. Which distribution models that count?
notes.back: C) Binomial distribution.
notes.choices:
A) Poisson distribution
B) Exponential distribution
C) Binomial distribution
D) Normal distribution
notes.choicesExplained: A: Poisson models events in a time interval, not successes in a fixed number of trials. B: exponential models data with a constant failure rate, such as times to failure. D: normal is continuous, while this is a count of units out of 50.
notes.explanation: Each unit is a trial whose outcome is labelled success or failure (here, defective or not), with a fixed probability over a set number of trials.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 1.3.6.6.18 “Binomial Distribution”
notes.evidence: These outcomes are appropriately labeled "success" and "failure". The binomial distribution is used to obtain the probability of observing x successes in N trials, with the probability of success on a single trial denoted by p . The binomial distribution assumes that p is fixed for all trials.

notes.front: A help desk wants to model how many calls arrive in each 15-minute window. Which distribution is designed for this?
notes.back: B) Poisson distribution.
notes.choices:
A) Binomial distribution
B) Poisson distribution
C) t distribution
D) F distribution
notes.choicesExplained: A: binomial needs a fixed number of trials, each a success or failure. D and C: the F and t distributions supply critical regions for tests and confidence intervals; they are not models for counts.
notes.explanation: The Poisson distribution models the number of events occurring within a given time interval.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 1.3.6.6.19 “Poisson Distribution”
notes.evidence: The Poisson distribution is used to model the number of events occurring within a given time interval.

notes.front: What happens to the t distribution as its shape parameter ν becomes large?
notes.back: It approaches the normal distribution; the approximation is quite good for ν > 30.
notes.explanation: Its curves share the normal's general shape and differ mainly in the heaviness of the tails.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 1.3.6.6.4 “t Distribution”
notes.evidence: These plots all have a similar shape. The difference is in the heaviness of the tails. In fact, the t distribution with ν equal to 1 is a Cauchy distribution. The t distribution approaches a normal distribution as ν becomes large. The approximation is quite good for values of ν > 30.

notes.front: A team wants to test whether a population's standard deviation equals a specified value. Which distribution supplies the critical region?
notes.back: B) Chi-square distribution.
notes.choices:
A) Poisson distribution
B) Chi-square distribution
C) Exponential distribution
D) Binomial distribution
notes.choicesExplained: A, C and D model data (counts, failure times, successes) rather than supplying critical regions for a test of a standard deviation.
notes.explanation: The handbook names the test of whether a population's standard deviation equals a pre-specified value as a common use of the chi-square distribution.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 1.3.6.6.6 “Chi-Square Distribution”
notes.evidence: The chi-square distribution is used in many cases for the critical regions for hypothesis tests and in determining confidence intervals. Two common examples are the chi-square test for independence in an RxC contingency table and the chi-square test to determine if the standard deviation of a population is equal to a pre-specified value.

notes.front: An engineer wants to test whether two machines' outputs have equal variances. Which distribution supplies the critical region?
notes.back: B) F distribution.
notes.choices:
A) Exponential distribution
B) F distribution
C) t distribution
D) Poisson distribution
notes.choicesExplained: A and D model data rather than supply critical regions for tests. C: the t distribution's most common use is testing a process mean, not comparing two variances.
notes.explanation: The handbook gives the F test of whether the variances of two populations are equal as a common use of the F distribution.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 1.3.6.6.5 “F Distribution”
notes.evidence: The F distribution is used in many cases for the critical regions for hypothesis tests and in determining confidence intervals. Two common examples are the analysis of variance and the F test to determine if the variances of two populations are equal.

notes.front: On a normal probability plot of cycle times, the points bend clearly away from the straight line. What does this indicate?
notes.back: B) The data depart from normality.
notes.choices:
A) The data are approximately normal
B) The data depart from normality
C) The process mean has shifted over time
D) The sample is too small to plot
notes.choicesExplained: A: approximately normal data would form a roughly straight line. C: the plot compares the data with a normal distribution; it does not show time order. D: nothing in the plot's shape says the sample is too small.
notes.explanation: Departures from the straight line indicate departures from normality.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 1.3.3.21 “Normal Probability Plot”
notes.evidence: The data are plotted against a theoretical normal distribution in such a way that the points should form an approximate straight line. Departures from this straight line indicate departures from normality.

notes.front: What does a run chart show that a histogram does not?
notes.back: The time order of the observations.
notes.explanation: A histogram summarises how the values are distributed and loses the order in which they arrived; a run chart plots them in time sequence.
notes.source: LeanOhio (Ohio Department of Administrative Services), Lean Six Sigma Terminology, ver. 2, “Run Chart”, p. 12
